newsitem.title: USA: Megan's killer was raped by father, brother says.
newsitem.headline: Megan's killer was raped by father, brother says.

text.p: Jesse Timmendequas, convicted of the rape and murder of 7-year-old Megan Kanka, was the target of sexual attacks by his own father, Timmendequas' brother said Tuesday in the penalty phase of the trial.
The attack on Kanka terrified a community and inspired the so-called Megan's Law for convicted child molesters.

In a move defence lawyers hope will keep his brother from being executed, Paul Timmendequas said in videotaped testimony that their father began sexually abusing them when Jesse Timmendequas, now 36, was 6 or 7.
Crying, shaking and chain smoking cigarettes, Paul, 33, said his the father would beat them, force them to perform oral sex on him and sodomize Jesse.
The brother's videotaped testimony was presented to a silent courtroom in Mercer County Superior Court.
Jesse Timmendequas was convicted last month of raping, sodomizing and killing Megan in 1994. He was a twice-convicted sex offender who lived across the street from her.
The crime in New Jersey's Hamilton Township touched off a public outcry. Megan's parents said they had not known their neighbour's background.

Megan's Law was the result of the Kanka family's impassioned campaigning. Originally it required such offenders to register with authorities and empowered authorities to notify the public about those they regarded as posing the highest risk.

However, a series of rulings left the state with the power to require registration but not to notify the public, and that aspect of the law is being challenged in federal court. Critics say Megan's Law violates the Constitution by punishing criminals after they have served their prison sentence.
Most other states also have versions of Megan's Law, and in 1996 President Clinton signed a federal law making it easier for residents to get information about released sex offenders.
Prosecutors soughteeking the death penalty for Timmendequas. Under a new state law, he could be sentenced to life in prison.
Timmendequas' lawyers are trying to spare him the death penalty by portraying a childhood of abuse and neglect that left him mentally ill.
